content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has outlined several research priorities and recommendations for malaria vector control and preventive chemotherapy. These recommendations aim to address gaps in evidence and improve the effectiveness of interventions in various settings, including areas with high insecticide resistance, humanitarian emergencies, and low malaria transmission. Below is a detailed explanation of the key points: Vector Control Research Priorities 1. Insecticide-Treated Nets (ITNs): Assess the impact of pyrethroid-only ITNs on malaria incidence (infection or clinical disease) and prevalence, particularly in areas with high pyrethroid resistance. Compare the effectiveness and durability of different types of ITNs. Evaluate the effectiveness of ITNs in settings with residual or outdoor malaria transmission. Investigate the impact of ITNs in malaria transmission hotspots and elimination settings. 2. Pyrethroid-PBO Nets: Gather evidence on the impact of pyrethroid-PBO nets in areas where vector resistance mechanisms are not oxidase-based and in regions with lower malaria transmission intensity. Study the durability of pyrethroid-PBO nets. 3. ITNs in Humanitarian Emergencies: Determine the impact of ITNs during the acute phase of humanitarian emergencies, where logistical challenges and differing priorities may affect implementation. 4. Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS): Investigate the impact of IRS in urbanized areas with changing housing designs. Evaluate alternative IRS delivery methods, such as partial wall treatments versus full surface treatments. Assess the impact of outdoor residual spraying and other innovative application methods, such as painting or slow-acting active ingredients. Study the effectiveness of proactive versus reactive IRS delivery in low-transmission areas. 5. Co-deployment of IRS and ITNs: Examine the impact of combining IRS and ITNs versus using ITNs or IRS alone, particularly in areas with mosquito populations resistant to non-pyrethroid insecticides. Assess the acceptability of combining IRS and ITNs among households and communities. Develop tools to monitor the quality of IRS and ITN interventions. 6. Larviciding and Habitat Modification: Evaluate the impact of larviciding on malaria incidence and prevalence, as well as potential unintended consequences. Explore new technologies for identifying aquatic mosquito habitats. Study the effects of larval habitat manipulation, including changes to water flow, volume, sunlight penetration, and salinity. 7. Larvivorous Fish: Investigate the impact and potential harms of using larvivorous fish for malaria control. 8. Repellents: Generate evidence on the impact of topical repellents for high-risk populations, such as migrants, refugees, forest-goers, and outdoor sleepers. Study the effectiveness of repellents in African settings and against Plasmodium vivax malaria. Assess the acceptability, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and equity of repellent use. Evaluate whether repellents divert malaria mosquitoes from treated to untreated areas. 9. Insecticide-Treated Clothing: Determine the impact and potential harms of insecticide-treated clothing in the general population. Develop formulations to improve the durability of insecticidal efficacy. 10. Spatial and Airborne Repellents: Study the impact of spatial or airborne repellents on malaria incidence and prevalence. Develop long-lasting spatial repellent formulations. 11. Space Spraying: Assess the impact of space spraying, particularly in emergency situations. 12. House Modifications: Evaluate the impact of house screening and other housing modifications on malaria outcomes, either alone or in combination with other interventions. Study the cost-effectiveness and community acceptance of house screening. 13. Insecticide Resistance Management: Investigate the impact of different strategies for managing insecticide resistance, such as insecticide rotations and mosaics. Assess the effects of insecticide resistance on key malaria outcomes, including mortality and infection prevalence. Preventive Chemotherapy 1. Chemoprevention and Chemoprophylaxis: Chemoprevention involves administering full therapeutic courses of antimalarial medicines at prescheduled intervals to treat existing infections and prevent new ones in endemic areas. Chemoprophylaxis typically involves sub-therapeutic doses of antimalarials to prevent new infections, primarily for non-immune travelers to endemic regions. 2. Current WHO Recommendations for Chemoprevention: Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp): Administer antimalarial medicines at predetermined intervals during pregnancy to reduce maternal anemia, placental infection, and low birth weight. Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC): Provide antimalarial medicines to children during high-transmission seasons. Perennial Malaria Chemoprevention (PMC): Previously known as intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi). Post-Discharge Malaria Chemoprevention (PDMC): Administer antimalarials to children recently discharged from hospital care. Mass Drug Administration (MDA): Use antimalarials to reduce malaria burden and transmission in specific settings. 3. IPTp with Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (SP): SP is widely used for malaria chemoprevention during pregnancy due to its efficacy, safety, and low cost. IPTp-SP should start in the second trimester (after week 13) and be administered at least one month apart during antenatal care visits, with a minimum of three doses recommended. SP remains effective even in areas with high SP resistance, as it reduces maternal anemia and low birth weight. 4. Drug Resistance and IPTp-SP: While SP use may select for antifolate resistance mutations, there is no convincing evidence of selection favoring key mutations that compromise IPTp-SP efficacy. IPTp-SP should continue to be used in areas of high SP resistance until more effective alternatives are available. 5. Implementation Considerations: Information about IPTp should be accessible to pregnant women, and their consent should be obtained before administration. Alternative delivery methods, such as community health workers, may be explored to address inequities in antenatal care access. 6. Research priorities include evaluating the effectiveness of vector control interventions, addressing insecticide resistance, and optimizing chemoprevention strategies. These efforts aim to reduce malaria burden, improve pregnancy outcomes, and protect vulnerable populations in endemic and emergency settings.
